ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
As shown in the figure, a small object (which can be considered as a point mass) is placed on a thin cardboard on a table. A constant horizontal force $F$ is applied to the right to pull the cardboard. Depending on the magnitude of the force, the motion of the cardboard and the small object will vary. The mass of the cardboard is $m_{1}=0.1\mathrm{kg}$, the mass of the small object is $m_{2}=0.4\mathrm{kg}$, and the distance between the small object and the right edge of the table is $d=0.15\mathrm{m}$. The coefficient of kinetic friction between all contact surfaces is $\mu=0.2$, and the maximum static friction is equal to the kinetic friction. The acceleration due to gravity is $g=10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$.

1. When the small object moves together with the cardboard, the magnitude of the frictional force exerted by the tabletop on the cardboard.
2. Under what condition does the pulling force $F$ satisfy for the small object to experience relative sliding with the cardboard?
3. If the pulling force acts for 0.3 seconds and the cardboard is just pulled out from under the small object, determine whether the small object will remain on the table through calculation.
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
$1\mathrm{N}$
$F>2\mathrm{N}$
Small objects will not remain on the tabletop. Do not add any other content.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a small block placed on a thin cardboard sheet, and the cardboard sheet is placed on a tabletop; the cardboard sheet is subjected to a horizontal pulling force F to the right. In the figure, d marks the horizontal distance from the small block's initial position to the right edge of the table. Reasoning: When the small block and the cardboard sheet move together, regard the two as a whole. The table's supporting force on the cardboard sheet equals the total gravity (m1+m2)g, so the magnitude of the sliding friction force of the table on the cardboard sheet is μ(m1+m2)g=0.2×(0.1+0.4)×10=1 N. If there is no relative sliding, the overall acceleration a=(F-1)/(m1+m2)=(F-1)/0.5. The small block can only be accelerated by static friction, and the maximum acceleration corresponding to maximum static friction is μg=2 m/s², so it is necessary that a≤2, namely (F-1)/0.5≤2, giving F≤2 N. Therefore relative sliding requires F>2 N. If the cardboard sheet is just pulled out at 0.3 s, the small block is accelerated to the right by friction on the cardboard sheet, a=μg=2 m/s², displacement s1=1/2×2×0.3²=0.09 m, and velocity v=2×0.3=0.6 m/s. After the cardboard sheet is pulled out, the small block is decelerated by friction on the tabletop, and the acceleration magnitude is still 2 m/s², with stopping distance s2=v²/(2a)=0.6²/(2×2)=0.09 m. The total rightward displacement s1+s2=0.18 m>d=0.15 m, so the small block will slide off the tabletop and cannot remain on the tabletop.

method.method_draft: First read the figure as a block on a thin cardboard sheet on a tabletop, with the sheet pulled horizontally to the right by force F, and with d marking the block's initial horizontal distance to the right table edge. From the text take m1=0.1 kg, m2=0.4 kg, mu=0.2, g=10 m/s^2, d=0.15 m, and the 0.3 s pull time. Treat the cardboard-plus-object as one body when they move together: the table supports both masses, so the tabletop friction on the cardboard is mu(m1+m2)g=1 N. For no slipping, the common acceleration would be a=(F-1)/(m1+m2); the object can be accelerated only by static friction up to mu m2 g, so require m2 a <= mu m2 g. This gives F<=2 N, hence relative sliding requires F>2 N. For the 0.3 s pullout case, once sliding occurs the object's acceleration while on cardboard is mu g=2 m/s^2, so in 0.3 s it moves 0.5*2*(0.3)^2=0.09 m and has speed 0.6 m/s. After the cardboard leaves, table friction decelerates it at 2 m/s^2, giving stopping distance 0.6^2/(2*2)=0.09 m. Total possible rightward travel is 0.18 m>d, so it will not remain on the table.

From the text extract m1, m2, mu, g, d, and t=0.3 s. Use a limiting-acceleration argument: if the object is to remain stuck to the cardboard, the largest acceleration it can share is a_max=mu g=2 m/s^2, because horizontal static friction is its only accelerating force. Meanwhile the combined object-cardboard system must overcome table friction mu(m1+m2)g=1 N, so at the slip threshold F = table friction + (m1+m2)a_max = 1+0.5*2=2 N; therefore slip occurs for F>2 N. The tabletop friction asked in part 1 is just the same external friction on the cardboard when supporting both masses, namely 1 N. For the final check, interpret 'cardboard is just pulled out from under the object' as meaning the object has been sliding on cardboard for 0.3 s under kinetic friction, so its acceleration is mu g. Compare its total stopping distance from the initial position to the table-edge distance: during the pull it travels 0.09 m; after transfer to the table it still has kinetic energy equivalent to another 0.09 m of sliding under the same friction; since 0.18 m exceeds 0.15 m, it falls off.

method.method_draft: First describe the image: a small block rests on a thin sheet on a table, the sheet is pulled to the right by F, and the marked distance d is from the block's initial position to the right edge of the table. From the written data use m1=0.1 kg, m2=0.4 kg, mu=0.2, g=10 m/s^2, d=0.15 m, and pull time 0.3 s. Draw separate free-body diagrams for the cardboard and the object. When there is no relative motion, the table's normal on the cardboard equals (m1+m2)g, so the tabletop's friction force on the cardboard is mu(m1+m2)g=1 N. For the impending-slip condition, set the needed friction on the object equal to its maximum value: f=m2 a=mu m2 g. The cardboard-object pair under external forces F and the 1 N table friction has acceleration a=(F-1)/(m1+m2). Substitution gives F=2 N as the boundary, so sliding needs F>2 N. For the last part use impulse/energy language: while the cardboard is being pulled out, kinetic friction gives the block acceleration 2 m/s^2 for 0.3 s, so its speed becomes 0.6 m/s and its displacement is 0.09 m. Then, after contacting the table, friction removes its kinetic energy: (1/2)m2 v^2 = mu m2 g s, giving s=0.09 m. Since 0.09+0.09=0.18 m is greater than the imaged edge distance d=0.15 m, the object cannot remain on the tabletop.

Image description: The figure shows a small block resting on a thin cardboard sheet, and the cardboard lies on a tabletop. A horizontal pulling force F is applied to the cardboard toward the right. The marked distance d is from the small block’s initial position to the right edge of the table.

Reasoning: Given m1=0.1 kg, m2=0.4 kg, mu=0.2, g=10 m/s^2, d=0.15 m, and pull time t=0.3 s.

1. When the object and cardboard move together, treat them as a combined system vertically supported by the table through the cardboard. The normal force from the tabletop on the cardboard is N=(m1+m2)g=(0.1+0.4)*10=5 N. Therefore the tabletop friction on the cardboard is f=mu N=0.2*5=1 N.

2. For no relative sliding, the object must be accelerated by static friction from the cardboard. The maximum friction on the object is fmax=mu m2 g=0.2*0.4*10=0.8 N, so the maximum acceleration the object can share is amax=fmax/m2=0.8/0.4=2 m/s^2. For the cardboard-object system, the horizontal external forces are F rightward and 1 N tabletop friction leftward, so a=(F-1)/(m1+m2)=(F-1)/0.5. At the slipping threshold, (F-1)/0.5=2, giving F=2 N. Thus relative sliding occurs when F>2 N.

3. While the cardboard is being pulled out from under the object, kinetic friction accelerates the object rightward with a=mu g=2 m/s^2 for 0.3 s. Its speed becomes v=at=2*0.3=0.6 m/s, and its displacement is x1=1/2*a*t^2=0.5*2*(0.3)^2=0.09 m. After the cardboard is gone, the object slides on the tabletop and is slowed by kinetic friction. Using energy, (1/2)m2 v^2=mu m2 g s, so s=v^2/(2mu g)=0.36/(2*0.2*10)=0.09 m. The total displacement before stopping would be x1+s=0.09+0.09=0.18 m, which is greater than d=0.15 m. Therefore the small object will not remain on the table.

raw_record.original_question:
As shown in the figure, a small object (which can be considered as a point mass) is placed on a thin cardboard on a table. A constant horizontal force $F$ is applied to the right to pull the cardboard. Depending on the magnitude of the force, the motion of the cardboard and the small object will vary. The mass of the cardboard is $m_{1}=0.1\mathrm{kg}$, the mass of the small object is $m_{2}=0.4\mathrm{kg}$, and the distance between the small object and the right edge of the table is $d=0.15\mathrm{m}$. The coefficient of kinetic friction between all contact surfaces is $\mu=0.2$, and the maximum static friction is equal to the kinetic friction. The acceleration due to gravity is $g=10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$.

1. When the small object moves together with the cardboard, the magnitude of the frictional force exerted by the tabletop on the cardboard.
2. Under what condition does the pulling force $F$ satisfy for the small object to experience relative sliding with the cardboard?
3. If the pulling force acts for 0.3 seconds and the cardboard is just pulled out from under the small object, determine whether the small object will remain on the table through calculation.
raw_record.answer:
$1\mathrm{N}$
$F>2\mathrm{N}$
Small objects will not remain on the tabletop. Do not add any other content

Image description: The figure shows a small block placed on a thin cardboard sheet, and the cardboard sheet is placed on a tabletop; the cardboard sheet is subjected to a horizontal pulling force F to the right. In the figure, d marks the horizontal distance from the small block's initial position to the right edge of the table.

Reasoning: When the small block and the cardboard sheet move together, regard the two as a whole. The table's supporting force on the cardboard sheet equals the total gravity (m1+m2)g, so the magnitude of the sliding friction force of the table on the cardboard sheet is μ(m1+m2)g=0.2×(0.1+0.4)×10=1 N. If there is no relative sliding, the overall acceleration a=(F-1)/(m1+m2)=(F-1)/0.5. The small block can only be accelerated by static friction, and the maximum acceleration corresponding to maximum static friction is μg=2 m/s², so it is necessary that a≤2, namely (F-1)/0.5≤2, giving F≤2 N. Therefore relative sliding requires F>2 N. If the cardboard sheet is just pulled out at 0.3 s, the small block is accelerated to the right by friction on the cardboard sheet, a=μg=2 m/s², displacement s1=1/2×2×0.3²=0.09 m, and velocity v=2×0.3=0.6 m/s. After the cardboard sheet is pulled out, the small block is decelerated by friction on the tabletop, and the acceleration magnitude is still 2 m/s², with stopping distance s2=v²/(2a)=0.6²/(2×2)=0.09 m. The total rightward displacement s1+s2=0.18 m>d=0.15 m, so the small block will slide off the tabletop and cannot remain on the tabletop.
